reading.prompt: Why did the new job initially appeal to Nina?
options: It offered a much higher salary
reading.passage: Nina moved to Oxford last year after accepting a position with a small design company. At first, the main attraction was the shorter commute: the new office was only twenty minutes from the flat. However, the biggest change was not professional. Nina joined a local community kitchen that prepares evening meals for older residents twice a month. The first session felt unfamiliar because everyone else seemed to know one another, but the coordinator gave each new volunteer a simple task and introduced them to the team. After several months, Nina began organising the shopping list and contacting local businesses for donated ingredients. The role required more planning than expected, yet it also improved confidence when speaking to strangers. One local café later offered to supply bread every Friday, which reduced the group’s costs. Nina still enjoys the job in design, but says the community work has made the city feel like home. The experience also changed future plans: instead of moving again soon, Nina now wants to stay in Oxford and take a short evening course in project management.

options.text: This may mean checking official websites, asking a provider questions or reading recent customer information.
Otherwise, an attractive headline price can hide conditions that matter later.
This is particularly helpful when several decisions have to be made during the same week.
For example, an email can record the agreed time, price and person responsible.
They also give you a chance to notice problems before they become expensive.
Some people prefer to decide without checking any details.
A long technical document is always the best starting point.
The cheapest choice is therefore automatically the safest.

reading.passage: When adults make a change connected with transport, the first step is often gathering reliable information. [1] It is also useful to compare more than one option rather than accepting the first offer. [2] A simple written list can make costs, dates and responsibilities easier to see. [3] If another person is involved, confirming the final arrangement in writing prevents misunderstandings. [4] Small practical checks may seem slow at the beginning, but they usually save time later. [5] For that reason, good planning is less about doing everything immediately and more about making each next step clear.

listening.prompt: How much is the transfer fee?

listening.prompt: When is the restaurant booking?

listening.prompt: What needs repairing?

listening.prompt: Where will the work meeting take place?

listening.prompt: Why did the speaker change jobs?
listening.transcript: I liked my old team, but I spent nearly two hours travelling each day. The new role pays about the same, but the office is fifteen minutes from home.

listening.prompt: What was the main problem at the hotel?
listening.transcript: The staff were helpful and breakfast was included. My room, however, faced a busy road and I found it difficult to sleep.

listening.prompt: Why did the customer call technical support?
listening.transcript: My internet connection was fine and the laptop screen worked normally. I called because the password reset link kept expiring.

listening.prompt: What advice did the nurse give?
listening.transcript: The nurse said I did not need an urgent appointment. She suggested resting, drinking plenty of water and calling again if I felt worse.

listening.prompt: What does the speaker like about the community event?
listening.transcript: I enjoy the neighbourhood food festival because I can walk there and there is no entrance fee. It is busy, but that is part of the atmosphere.

listening.prompt: Why did the customer choose this repair company?
listening.transcript: Another company offered a slightly lower price, but this one could send an engineer the next morning, which mattered more to me.

listening.prompt: Why did Nina reduce working days?
listening.transcript: Interviewer: Nina, you recently started working four days a week. Why did you make the change? Nina: I wanted more time for family and a professional course. Interviewer: Was the lower salary difficult? Nina: At first I worried about it, but I reduced commuting and lunch costs, so the difference was smaller than expected. Interviewer: What has surprised you most? Nina: I am more focused on the days I work. I also plan my week more carefully. Interviewer: Would you recommend the arrangement to everyone? Nina: Not automatically. It depends on income, responsibilities and whether the employer can offer flexibility. Interviewer: What will you do after the course? Nina: I hope to apply for a role with more responsibility, but I want to keep one weekday free if possible.
